name: Menstrual Cycle, Hormone and Pelvic-Symptom Support Guidance
purpose: Provide cycle-, hormone-, androgen-, pelvic-, and fertility-context questions, local symptom tracking, low-risk support options, safety escalation, and clinical follow-up prompts when explicitly relevant. This is not a diagnostic or treatment engine.

intake_schema.title: Optional cycle and hormone context
intake_schema.description: Use this small, private, self-reported context record to organize cycle timing, symptoms, and exact hormone or contraceptive product details. Leave any field blank when it is not relevant.
intake_schema.privacy_note: Stored locally per DNA profile. These values are phenotype and medication context, not genetic evidence, and they do not establish anatomy, identity, pregnancy, hormone levels, a diagnosis, or treatment response.

groups.title: Cycle timing and symptoms
groups.description: Prospective timing is more useful than a single retrospective impression. Record symptom-free days as well as difficult days when possible.

groups.title: Measured hormones and treatment timing
groups.description: Use when a person already has hormone or related laboratory results. Record the test date, units, reference range, cycle or bleeding timing, exact product timing, and clinician interpretation instead of asking DNA to estimate a current level.

groups.title: Androgen, prostate, testicular, and measured-lab context
groups.description: Use only when relevant to the selected body or care goal. Record symptoms and measured findings without turning them into a DNA diagnosis.

groups.title: Hormone or contraceptive product review
groups.description: Use the package, pharmacy, or prescribing label. Do not guess whether a product contains estrogen, progestin, progesterone, or another active ingredient.

groups.title: Clinical questions and follow-up
groups.description: Capture what should be discussed with a clinician; do not turn a suspected condition into a confirmed diagnosis.

fields.label: First day of most recent bleeding
fields.placeholder: YYYY-MM-DD
fields.help: Optional. Day 1 means the first day of menstrual bleeding when that definition is relevant to the person.

fields.label: Typical cycle length (days)
fields.help: Optional; record an approximate value if cycles are regular enough to estimate.

fields.label: Typical bleeding length (days)
fields.placeholder: e.g. 5
fields.help: Optional; also note unusual or changing bleeding in the symptom field.

fields.label: When symptoms usually begin
fields.placeholder: e.g. about 5 days before bleeding
fields.help: Describe timing relative to bleeding or another event; do not label the cause from DNA.

fields.label: When symptoms usually ease
fields.placeholder: e.g. within 2 days after bleeding starts
fields.help: Include symptom-free days when known.

fields.label: Mood, behavior, or need-for-space symptoms
fields.placeholder: e.g. irritability, anger, avoidance, need for quiet, anxiety, depression, relationship or work impact
fields.help: Describe what is observed and its impact without using the field to diagnose PMDD or a psychiatric condition.

fields.label: Need-for-space or communication pattern
fields.placeholder: e.g. asks to be left alone, avoids contact, prefers a check-in later, or support that helps
fields.help: Record the person's words, timing, boundaries, and support preferences without treating avoidance as a character judgment or assigning a hormone cause.

fields.label: Pain, bleeding, or headache symptoms
fields.placeholder: e.g. cramps, pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, headache, possible aura, faintness
fields.help: Record severity and functional impact when useful; urgent symptoms still need timely care.

fields.label: Androgen, prostate, testicular, or urinary symptoms
fields.placeholder: e.g. libido, erectile function, energy, urinary changes, testicular pain/swelling, or another concern
fields.help: Optional and body-context neutral. Sudden severe testicular pain, a new lump, acute urinary retention, or severe symptoms need timely medical care.

fields.label: Measured hormone or related lab results
fields.placeholder: e.g. test name, date, value, units, reference range, and clinician interpretation
fields.help: Measured results are clinical context; a DNA marker does not replace testing or establish current hormone levels.

fields.label: Cycle or treatment timing for labs
fields.placeholder: e.g. cycle day or bleeding status, time of day, time since last dose, and current product
fields.help: Timing can affect interpretation. Use the laboratory report and clinician guidance; do not infer a level or treatment response from DNA.

fields.label: Fertility or family-building context
fields.placeholder: e.g. planning, evaluation, preservation, partner factors, or leave blank
fields.help: Optional user-supplied context. DNA cannot diagnose infertility or predict fertility outcomes.

fields.label: Exact product name
fields.placeholder: e.g. product name from package or pharmacy record
fields.help: A DNA file cannot identify a medication product.

fields.label: Active ingredient(s) exactly as labeled
fields.placeholder: e.g. norethindrone 0.35 mg; or estradiol / progestin
fields.help: This is the key field for distinguishing a product label from a belief about estrogen or progesterone exposure.

fields.label: Route, dose, and schedule
fields.placeholder: e.g. oral, one tablet daily; or patch changed weekly
fields.help: Include the prescribed schedule; do not change it from a DNA result.

fields.label: Started or changed on
fields.placeholder: YYYY-MM-DD
fields.help: Useful for comparing symptom or bleeding changes before and after a product change.

fields.label: Goal for the product
fields.placeholder: e.g. contraception, fewer or lighter periods, pain control, hormone therapy, another clinician-defined goal
fields.help: A product can have more than one goal; the goal is user-supplied context.

fields.label: Benefits noticed
fields.placeholder: e.g. less bleeding, fewer painful days, no new adverse effects
fields.help: Record observed benefits separately from genetic interpretation.

fields.label: Adverse effects or none noticed
fields.placeholder: e.g. headache, spotting, mood change, or none noticed
fields.help: No new adverse effects is useful information, but it does not identify the product composition or prove future safety.

fields.label: Question or belief to verify
fields.placeholder: e.g. I think this is progesterone-only; please verify against the label
fields.help: Keep uncertainty visible. The tool should compare this statement with the exact label, not treat it as established fact.

fields.label: Clinical questions or findings to discuss
fields.placeholder: e.g. heavy bleeding, suspected adenomyosis, CBC/ferritin, ultrasound, migraine assessment
fields.help: Use this to prepare for clinical care; a consumer DNA file cannot diagnose or exclude adenomyosis.

do_not_infer: Do not infer current estrogen, progesterone, progestin, allopregnanolone, ovulation, pregnancy, or medication response from DNA or from a symptom pattern.
Do not infer that a product is contraceptive, estrogen-containing, or progestin-only without the exact label or prescribing record.
Do not infer PMDD, adenomyosis, endometriosis, PCOS, infertility, or a psychiatric diagnosis from these fields or from a DNA marker.
Do not infer hypogonadism, prostate disease, testicular disease, fertility, or anatomy from a DNA marker or from a selected context.
Do not infer personality, intent, relationship meaning, or a fixed character trait from cyclic withdrawal, avoidance, irritability, or a request for space.

diary_schema.title: Optional daily cycle and symptom diary
diary_schema.description: Use this local diary to compare bleeding, symptoms, functioning, sleep, stress, and treatment timing across cycles. Include lower-symptom days as well as difficult days.
diary_schema.privacy_note: Stored locally per DNA profile with a bounded history. Diary entries are self-reported observations, not genotype evidence, hormone measurements, or a diagnosis.

fields.label: Date
fields.placeholder: YYYY-MM-DD
fields.help: Required. Use the local calendar date for the observation.

fields.label: Cycle day (optional)
fields.help: Optional and approximate; do not use it to infer ovulation or hormone levels.

fields.label: Bleeding or spotting level (0–4)
fields.placeholder: 0 none · 4 heavy
fields.help: 0 none, 1 spotting, 2 light, 3 moderate, 4 heavy by the person’s own consistent description.

fields.label: Mood or behavior impact (0–4)
fields.placeholder: 0 baseline · 4 severe impact
fields.help: Use the same personal scale over time; describe the actual experience in the notes and seek timely help for safety concerns.

fields.label: Pain or headache impact (0–4)
fields.placeholder: 0 none · 4 severe impact
fields.help: Use the same personal scale over time; sudden severe pain or neurologic symptoms need timely care.

fields.label: Mood, behavior, or need-for-space notes
fields.placeholder: e.g. more irritable, wants quiet, avoidant, relationship/work impact, or baseline day
fields.help: Record observations and impact without labeling PMDD, a psychiatric condition, or a hormone cause.

fields.label: Pain, bleeding, or headache notes
fields.placeholder: e.g. cramps, pelvic pain, clots, migraine features, faintness, or no symptoms
fields.help: Record details that may help a clinician assess bleeding, pelvic pain, or headache patterns.

fields.label: Sleep, stress, food, activity, or medication context
fields.placeholder: e.g. sleep change, major stress, missed dose, supplement, meal, alcohol, or unusual activity
fields.help: Context can change symptoms; record exact products and timing when relevant rather than attributing the change to DNA.

fields.label: Functioning, support, or safety notes
fields.placeholder: e.g. missed work, requested space, support that helped, or safety concern requiring care
fields.help: Use concrete impact and support needs. Immediate danger or self-harm risk requires local emergency or crisis support.

do_not_infer: Do not infer estrogen, progesterone, ovulation, PMDD, adenomyosis, endometriosis, or medication response from diary scores or timing.
Do not treat a missing diary entry as a symptom-free day or a normal result.
Do not use diary patterns to start, stop, dose, or switch medication or supplements.
Do not infer personality, intent, relationship meaning, or a fixed character trait from cyclic withdrawal, avoidance, irritability, or a request for space.

context_options.label: Menstrual cycle / PMS / PMDD symptoms
context_options.description: Use when the person reports an ongoing menstrual cycle or recurring cycle-linked symptoms.

context_options.label: Cycle-linked pain or migraine
context_options.description: Use only when a person reports recurring pelvic pain, headache, or migraine around a user-supplied bleeding or cycle pattern. This route does not infer menstruation, anatomy, migraine, or contraceptive safety from DNA.

context_options.label: Cyclic mood, irritability or need-for-space symptoms
context_options.description: Use when the person reports recurring irritability, anger, avoidance, anxiety, depression, or a need for more space around a suspected cycle window. This is a symptom-timing route, not a PMDD diagnosis or a hormone-level inference.

context_options.label: Ovarian / reproductive care
context_options.description: Use when ovarian or reproductive care is relevant, without assuming a cycle, anatomy, fertility, or pregnancy status.

context_options.label: Uterine / pelvic symptoms
context_options.description: Use when bleeding, pelvic pain, or a uterine evaluation is relevant.

context_options.label: Suspected adenomyosis / heavy-bleeding workup
context_options.description: Use when the person reports a concern about adenomyosis or symptoms that warrant a uterine/pelvic workup. Consumer DNA cannot diagnose or exclude adenomyosis; route to symptom history, examination, and clinically indicated imaging.

context_options.label: Androgen / prostate / testicular context
context_options.description: Use when androgen, prostate, testicular, or related reproductive context is relevant.

context_options.label: Menopause / hormone therapy
context_options.description: Use when menopause or hormone-therapy context is relevant; record the exact product and ingredients.

context_options.label: Exogenous hormone therapy / gender-affirming care
context_options.description: Use when estrogen, testosterone, progesterone/progestin, an antiandrogen, puberty suppression, or another prescribed hormone treatment is relevant. Record the exact product and monitoring context without assuming identity, anatomy, or goals.

context_options.label: Pregnancy / postpartum / lactation context
context_options.description: Use only when the person supplies this context; DNA does not establish pregnancy, postpartum timing, lactation, feeding goals, or medication safety.

context_options.label: Preconception / fertility evaluation
context_options.description: Use only when the person supplies a pregnancy-planning or fertility-evaluation goal. This route supports people with different bodies, partners, and family-building paths without inferring anatomy, identity, fertility, or pregnancy from DNA.

context_options.label: Not relevant / keep reproductive guidance hidden
context_options.description: Keep cycle and reproductive support hidden until relevant context is supplied.

principles: Cycle timing is phenotype information that must be recorded; a consumer DNA file cannot measure current estrogen, progesterone, allopregnanolone, ovulation, or uterine tissue.

In a natural ovulatory cycle, estradiol and progesterone generally fall during the late-luteal transition before bleeding. Symptoms can reflect sensitivity to hormone change rather than an estrogen spike.

Hormonal contraception can change bleeding and hormone patterns. Identify the exact product and active ingredients before discussing cycle effects; progestin is not the same chemical as endogenous progesterone.

Cyclic irritability, avoidance, anxiety, depression, pain, or bleeding are reasons to organize timing and clinical questions, not reasons to infer PMDD, adenomyosis, endometriosis, or a medication problem from DNA.

Cycle-linked pelvic pain, headache, or migraine should be tracked against bleeding and other symptoms; timing can guide clinical questions, but DNA cannot diagnose dysmenorrhea, menstrual-related migraine, or the cause of pelvic pain.

Food, supplement, sleep, and activity changes should be treated as small, reversible experiments based on the person's symptoms, diet, medications, allergies, labs, and goals; DNA does not establish a nutrient deficiency or a universal menstrual trigger.
When symptoms are present, use sleep, regular meals, hydration, and activity scaled to symptoms as general supportive options; do not present them as genotype-specific treatment.

domains.title: Cycle phase and symptom timing
domains.context: Map the first day of bleeding, symptom onset, symptom offset, and symptom-free days before assigning meaning to a cyclic pattern.
questions: What is day 1 of bleeding, and on which cycle days do irritability, avoidance, anxiety, depression, pain, or physical symptoms begin and end?
Do symptoms improve within a few days after bleeding starts, and are there symptom-free days in the follicular phase?
Has the pattern been recorded prospectively every day across at least two cycles, including symptom-free days?
support_options: Use a simple daily symptom score and bleeding log for at least two cycles; include sleep, major stressors, medication changes, and missed doses as context.

Do not label the late-luteal or menstrual transition an estrogen spike without clinician-directed hormone assessment; the natural-cycle direction is usually a fall in estradiol and progesterone before bleeding.
confirm_with: daily symptom tracking across at least two cycles
cycle and bleeding history
clinician review when symptoms impair relationships, work, safety, or daily function
red_flags: suicidal thoughts or feeling unsafe
severe mood symptoms with loss of functioning
new severe or sudden pelvic pain

domains.title: Measured hormones and treatment timing
domains.context: Current hormone levels and treatment response require clinical measurements interpreted with cycle or bleeding timing, exact product timing, age, relevant conditions, and the laboratory reference range.
questions: What exact test was measured, on what date, in what units, and with what laboratory reference range and clinician interpretation?
What was the cycle day or bleeding status, time of day, pregnancy possibility, and time since the last medication dose when the sample was taken?
What exact hormone or contraceptive product, dose, route, and schedule were in use, and what question should the result help answer?
support_options: Bring the laboratory report, medication or product label, cycle diary, and symptom timeline to the clinician; a DNA marker cannot substitute for a current hormone measurement.

Treat a single result as time- and context-dependent rather than as a permanent baseline. Ask the clinician whether repeat testing, a different cycle or treatment time, or another test is appropriate.
Do not start, stop, skip, or change hormone or contraceptive treatment based on a DNA result, a symptom theory, or an isolated lab value.
confirm_with: laboratory report with date, units, and reference range
cycle, bleeding, pregnancy, and treatment timing
clinician interpretation of the person's goal and symptoms
red_flags: severe or rapidly worsening symptoms
chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or one-sided leg swelling
suicidal thoughts or inability to remain safe

domains.title: Premenstrual mood-symptom support
domains.context: PMDD is assessed from a recurring symptom pattern and functional impact, not from one hormone level or SNP.
questions: Which symptoms recur before menses, how intense are they, and do they remit after bleeding begins?
Are symptoms present outside the premenstrual window, or do they represent worsening of an existing mood or anxiety condition?
Do anger, avoidance, depression, or anxiety create safety concerns or major impairment?
When irritability or avoidance peaks, what communication boundary or amount of space helps, and can the person still make safe decisions and meet essential responsibilities?
support_options: Bring the prospective symptom log to a clinician; it can help separate cyclic symptoms from persistent or overlapping conditions.
Keep supportive routines practical and non-punitive: regular sleep opportunity, regular meals, hydration, and symptom-scaled movement if tolerated.

During a lower-symptom period, agree on a simple communication plan: how to request space, when to check in, what practical support is welcome, and what to do if safety or functioning changes. This is a communication aid, not a diagnosis.

If the pattern causes meaningful impairment, ask a clinician about evidence-based options such as an SSRI, psychotherapy/CBT, or a carefully selected hormonal approach; the choice depends on medical history, goals, interactions, contraindications, and the exact product—not on a DNA marker.
If thoughts of self-harm or immediate danger occur, use local emergency or crisis support rather than waiting for a DNA interpretation.
confirm_with: prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two cycles
mental-health and primary-care review
clinician-directed treatment discussion, including medication interactions and contraindications
red_flags: suicidal ideation
self-harm risk
inability to remain safe

domains.title: Contraceptive and hormone-medication context
domains.context: A DNA file cannot identify a birth-control product, its dose, whether ovulation is suppressed, or whether a person is exposed to estrogen or progestin.
questions: What is the exact product name, active ingredient or ingredients, dose, schedule, and start date?
Is it progestin-only, combined estrogen-plus-progestin, an implant, an injection, an IUD, or another method?
Did the mood, bleeding, pain, or avoidance pattern change after starting, stopping, missing, or switching the product?
support_options: Use the package label or prescribing record when documenting the medication; do not infer its composition from the DNA report.

Record both benefits and unwanted effects—including no new adverse effects—after starting or changing the product; feeling well does not identify whether the method contains estrogen or progestin and does not replace routine follow-up.
Discuss benefits, risks, and alternatives with the prescriber or pharmacist; do not start, stop, or change dose from raw DNA or a symptom theory alone.
confirm_with: exact product label or prescribing record
active ingredients and dose
prescriber or pharmacist review
red_flags: possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding
severe new headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, or leg swelling while using a hormonal method
heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting, or weakness

domains.title: Heavy bleeding, pelvic pain and suspected adenomyosis
domains.context: Adenomyosis is a uterine tissue condition and is not diagnosed or excluded by a consumer SNP file.
questions: How many days does bleeding last, how heavy is it, and are there clots, dizziness, fatigue, or reduced exercise tolerance?
Is pelvic pain worsening, present between periods, or associated with pain during sex or bowel movements?
Has a clinician performed a pelvic examination or ordered imaging?
support_options: Record bleeding duration, approximate severity, pain score, and impact on work or daily activity for the clinical visit.
Ask about CBC and ferritin when bleeding is heavy or prolonged; do not begin iron solely because an HFE or other SNP was found.
Ask whether transvaginal ultrasound is appropriate; MRI may be considered when ultrasound is insufficient or a specialist recommends it.
confirm_with: CBC and ferritin when bleeding is heavy or prolonged
pelvic examination when appropriate
transvaginal ultrasound or MRI when clinically indicated
gynecology review
red_flags: very heavy bleeding with fainting, dizziness, weakness, or shortness of breath
severe or sudden pelvic pain
possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding

domains.title: Cycle-linked food, supplement, sleep and activity support
domains.context: Food, supplement, sleep, and activity patterns may influence how a person feels around a cycle, but a consumer DNA file cannot establish a deficiency, a food trigger, a supplement need, or a safe medication or exercise prescription.
questions: What food, caffeine, alcohol, salt, sugar, missed meals, hydration, sleep, or activity patterns change symptoms for this person, and which observations are repeated rather than assumed?

Are there heavy or prolonged periods, fatigue, dizziness, restricted eating, gastrointestinal symptoms, kidney or liver conditions, thyroid history, pregnancy possibility, allergies, or other factors that change nutrition and supplement safety?
What are the exact supplement, OTC, medication, and fortified-food labels, including iron, magnesium, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin A, vitamin B6, omega-3, iodine, and caffeine products?
What activity is realistic during symptomatic days, and are there pain, migraine, faintness, chest symptoms, unusual breathlessness, or recovery changes that should stop exercise and prompt care?
support_options: Start with ordinary balanced meals, regular meal timing, adequate fluids, sleep opportunity, and movement scaled to symptoms. Keep changes practical and reversible rather than using a restrictive hormone-detox or elimination plan.

For heavy bleeding or fatigue, ask whether CBC and ferritin are appropriate before taking iron; an HFE or other SNP is not proof of deficiency, and iron can be harmful when the problem is not deficiency.

Food sources of calcium and magnesium may fit some people's goals, but supplement trials should account for total intake, kidney function, pregnancy/lactation, and medication interactions. Do not use a DNA marker to justify a megadose.

If caffeine, alcohol, salt, sugar, or a specific food appears related to symptoms, test one modest change at a time while preserving adequate nutrition and tracking the result; do not assume the same trigger applies to everyone or infer an allergy from a symptom diary.
Regular activity may help some premenstrual symptoms, while symptomatic days may call for lower intensity or recovery. Stop for red flags and do not use genotype to clear maximal training.
confirm_with: food, symptom, sleep, activity, and medication-use diary
exact supplement and medication labels with total nutrient and caffeine exposure
CBC, ferritin, thyroid, kidney, or other labs only when clinically indicated
dietitian, primary-care, gynecology, neurology, or sports-medicine review as appropriate
red_flags: heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting, weakness, or shortness of breath
chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, new neurologic symptoms, or a first or worst sudden headache during activity
rapid weight loss, severe food restriction, repeated vomiting, dehydration, or symptoms of an eating disorder

domains.title: Cycle-linked pelvic pain, headache and migraine context
domains.context: A recurring relationship between bleeding or a user-supplied cycle and pain or headache is clinical context. A consumer DNA file cannot diagnose dysmenorrhea, menstrual-related migraine, migraine with aura, endometriosis, adenomyosis, or medication-overuse headache.
questions: On which days relative to bleeding or another cycle event do pelvic pain, cramps, headache, or migraine begin and end, and does the pattern repeat across at least two or three cycles?

For headaches, are there features such as throbbing pain, nausea, light or sound sensitivity, or aura symptoms such as flashing lights, blind spots, numbness, or speech difficulty? Has a clinician assessed the headache type?
Is pelvic pain worsening, lasting beyond the first days of bleeding, occurring between periods, or associated with pain during sex, bowel movements, urination, heavy bleeding, fever, or faintness?
How often are pain medicines, triptans, opioids, caffeine products, or other remedies used, and did symptoms change after starting, stopping, missing, or switching a medication or contraceptive?
support_options: Keep a daily headache, pain, bleeding, medication-use, and functional-impact diary for at least two cycles; prospective timing is more useful than relying on memory alone.

Use symptom-scaled movement, sleep opportunity, regular meals, hydration, and heat for cramps when tolerated; these are general supportive options, not genotype-specific treatment or a substitute for evaluation.

Ask a clinician about evidence-based acute or preventive treatment when symptoms impair life or recur predictably. Do not self-select NSAIDs, triptans, opioids, hormonal treatment, or supplements from a DNA result; pregnancy, kidney/liver disease, bleeding risk, interactions, and the exact product matter.

If migraine with aura is possible, document that distinction before discussing combined hormonal contraception; the exact method and medical history require clinician review, and DNA cannot clear or contraindicate a contraceptive method.
confirm_with: prospective headache, pain, bleeding, and medication-use diary across at least two cycles
clinical assessment of migraine with or without aura when relevant
exact medication and contraceptive product label with active ingredients
gynecology, primary-care, neurology, or pain review as appropriate
red_flags: first or worst sudden headache, new neurologic deficit, confusion, fainting, seizure, or severe vision or speech change
new or changing aura, severe headache during pregnancy or postpartum, or headache with markedly elevated blood pressure
severe or sudden pelvic pain, fever, possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding, or heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting, weakness, or shortness of breath

domains.title: General symptom-day support
domains.context: These are non-genotype-specific options to discuss or try safely while tracking symptoms; they are not a PMDD or adenomyosis treatment plan.
questions: Which basics are realistic during the symptomatic days: sleep opportunity, regular meals, hydration, gentle movement, or a quieter environment?
Are pain medicines, supplements, alcohol, caffeine, or other substances affecting symptoms or interacting with current medicines?
What support does the person want from others when symptoms are intense, and what communication boundary is safe and respectful?
support_options: Scale activity to symptoms and stop for concerning symptoms; DNA does not clear strenuous exercise during bleeding, pain, dizziness, or illness.
Use regular meals and hydration as practical supportive basics rather than restrictive elimination diets or hormone-detox claims.
Write a pre-agreed communication plan for difficult days, while treating safety, coercion, and interpersonal harm as separate concerns from genetics.
confirm_with: medication and supplement list
symptom and activity log
clinician review when symptoms are severe or worsening
red_flags: chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or new neurologic symptoms
suicidal thoughts or inability to remain safe
rapidly worsening pain or bleeding

domains.title: Androgen, prostate and testicular context
domains.context: A DNA report cannot measure testosterone, diagnose hypogonadism, determine fertility, or diagnose prostate or testicular disease.
questions: Is there current testosterone, androgen, prostate, fertility, or other hormone treatment? Record the exact product, active ingredients, dose, schedule, and start date.
Which symptoms or goals are relevant: libido, erectile function, energy, mood, fertility, urinary symptoms, testicular pain/swelling, or another concern?
Has a clinician evaluated symptoms with appropriate examination, laboratory testing, or imaging?
support_options: Track symptoms, sleep, training load, illness, medications, and treatment timing before attributing a change to DNA or hormones.
Discuss hormone or prostate concerns with the appropriate clinician; do not start, stop, or change hormone treatment from raw DNA or an online interpretation.
confirm_with: exact medication label and active ingredients
clinician assessment with laboratory testing or imaging when indicated
repeated early-morning testosterone testing only when a clinician is evaluating suspected deficiency
red_flags: sudden severe testicular or scrotal pain, especially with nausea or vomiting
new testicular lump, marked swelling, fever, or redness
acute urinary retention, blood in urine, or severe pelvic pain

domains.title: Exogenous hormone therapy and monitoring
domains.context: People with different bodies and goals may use estrogen, testosterone, progesterone/progestin, antiandrogens, puberty suppression, or other hormone therapy. DNA cannot measure current hormone levels, determine the right product or dose, or predict an individual response.
questions: What is the exact product name, active ingredient or ingredients, route, dose, schedule, indication or goal, and start date?
What clinician-directed monitoring is already being used, such as hormone levels, CBC/hematocrit, lipids, potassium/creatinine, prolactin, liver tests, or bone-health assessment when appropriate?
Did symptoms, bleeding, mood, pain, blood pressure, or other changes follow starting, stopping, missing, or switching the product?
support_options: Use the prescription label and treating clinician’s plan to identify composition and monitoring; do not infer hormone exposure from DNA, chromosome calls, or a symptom theory.
Track treatment timing, symptoms, and measured results to support shared decision-making; do not self-adjust, stop, or add hormone medication from this report.
Keep preventive screening, fertility-preservation, and anatomy-relevant care discussions with the appropriate clinician without assuming identity or anatomy from the genetic report.
confirm_with: exact medication label, active ingredients, route, dose, and schedule
clinician-directed hormone and safety-laboratory monitoring
treatment goals, symptoms, and adverse-effect review
red_flags: chest pain, sudden severe shortness of breath, fainting, or one-sided leg swelling
severe new headache, neurologic symptoms, or markedly elevated blood pressure
suicidal thoughts or inability to remain safe

domains.title: Pregnancy, postpartum and lactation safety context
domains.context: Pregnancy, postpartum recovery, lactation, chestfeeding, and feeding choices are user-supplied clinical contexts. DNA cannot establish pregnancy or postpartum status and cannot determine whether a medication or supplement is safe for a pregnant person, lactating person, or infant.
questions: What context applies now: trying to conceive, pregnant, postpartum, lactating/feeding, recently stopped feeding, or none of these? If relevant, what is the gestational or postpartum timing?
What are the exact medication, OTC, supplement, herbal, and topical-product names, active ingredients, dose, route, schedule, and prescriber instructions?

Has a clinician or pharmacist reviewed the medication list for pregnancy, postpartum, or infant-exposure considerations? If lactating/feeding, what infant age, prematurity, medical conditions, or feeding goals affect the review?
support_options: Use the exact product label and clinician/pharmacist review for pregnancy or lactation medication decisions; do not start, stop, skip, or substitute a medicine from genotype.

For lactation/feeding questions, look up the exact substance in a current medication-and-lactation reference such as LactMed and review the result with the treating clinician; do not assume that natural, topical, or prescribed means risk-free.

Keep prenatal, postpartum, and feeding care individualized: review supplements and total nutrient intake, monitor symptoms and measured labs when ordered, and preserve the person's feeding goals without treating DNA as a pregnancy or infant-safety test.
confirm_with: user-supplied pregnancy, postpartum, lactation/feeding, and conception context
exact medication, supplement, OTC, herbal, and topical-product labels
obstetric, primary-care, pediatric, lactation, or pharmacist review as appropriate
red_flags: heavy bleeding, fainting, severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or one-sided leg swelling during or after pregnancy
severe or worsening headache, vision changes, seizure, severe upper-abdominal pain, or markedly elevated blood pressure
fever with severe pelvic/abdominal pain, rapidly worsening illness, or suicidal thoughts

domains.title: Preconception and fertility-care context
domains.context: A fertility or preconception goal is a user-supplied care context. Consumer DNA may organize questions about known variants or family history, but it cannot measure ovarian reserve, ovulation, sperm quality, embryo health, pregnancy ability, or the safety of a medication or supplement.
questions: What is the goal and time horizon: preparing for a possible pregnancy, trying to conceive, fertility preservation, donor or assisted reproduction, or evaluation after difficulty conceiving?

Which body functions or partner factors are relevant to the person's goal, such as cycle/ovulation history, pelvic symptoms, semen or testicular history, prior pregnancies, or prior fertility treatment? Ask only what is relevant and do not assume anatomy, partner configuration, or family-building route.

What are the exact prescription, OTC, supplement, herbal, topical, nicotine, alcohol, and other exposure details, and what medical, surgical, psychiatric, family, or genetic history should the clinician know?
support_options: Arrange preconception or fertility counseling when the person wants it; bring the complete medication and supplement list, because products that seem unrelated to reproduction can still require review.

When infertility is being evaluated, ask how the relevant partners will be assessed concurrently and which least-invasive tests fit the person's history; the appropriate workup is not a consumer SNP panel.

Use the DNA report only to prompt questions about confirmed variants, family history, or clinically indicated carrier testing. Do not use common SNPs to predict fertility, ovarian reserve, sperm quality, miscarriage, embryo health, or pregnancy outcome.

Discuss nutrition, folic-acid/prenatal supplementation, activity, chronic-condition control, immunizations, and substance or environmental exposures with the clinician; do not let a common MTHFR or hormone marker override current public-health guidance.
confirm_with: preconception clinician or reproductive-endocrinology review
exact medication, supplement, herbal, and topical-product list
cycle/ovulation evaluation, semen analysis, or other testing only when clinically indicated
genetic counseling or validated clinical carrier testing when indicated
red_flags: severe or sudden pelvic, abdominal, testicular, or scrotal pain
